stories.title: From Field to Festival
stories.body: Korea's oldest popular drink — cloudy, slightly sparkling rice wine brewed for over a thousand years. For most of its history it was the farmer's daily fuel: cheap, nourishing, drunk straight from the bowl. Government rice rationing in the 1960s nearly killed it, but a 2009 craft revival brought it roaring back. Today's brewers experiment with everything from buckwheat to bananas.
stories.didYouKnow: The 2009 makgeolli boom started with Japanese tourists ordering it at Seoul restaurants — they made it cool again.

stories.title: Two Drinks, One Name
stories.body: Two completely different liquors hide behind the same word. Traditional 증류식 soju is rice spirit distilled in clay, brought to Andong by Mongol forces 700 years ago. Modern green-bottle 희석식 soju is a post-war invention — neutral spirit from sweet potato or tapioca, diluted with water. Same name, two universes.
stories.didYouKnow: Diluted soju started at 25% ABV in 1965 and has steadily dropped to around 16% today.

stories.title: The Drink of Kings
stories.body: When unfiltered rice brew sat undisturbed, the clear top layer was skimmed off and reserved for nobility and ancestral rites. That clear top became cheongju. Polished, dry, aromatic — closer to Japanese sake but with a fuller rice character. Still poured in jesa (ancestor ceremonies) today.
stories.didYouKnow: The Korean word 윗물 ('top water') literally refers to this practice of skimming clear cheongju from cloudy brew.

stories.title: When Liquor Was Medicine
stories.body: Yakju literally means 'medicinal liquor.' Joseon-era physicians infused rice wine with ginseng, pine pollen, deodeok root, and dozens of other herbs — many recipes survive in 17th-century texts like Donguibogam. Modern hits like Baekseju (백세주, 'hundred-year liquor') still lean into the heritage.
stories.didYouKnow: Joseon kings were prescribed yakju daily — court doctors logged each pour in the royal medical journals.

stories.title: Year-Long Patience
stories.body: Korea's home-fermentation tradition: fruit + sugar + spirit, sealed in a clay jar, forgotten for months or years. Maesilju (plum), bokbunjaju (black raspberry), yujaju (yuzu), meoruju (wild grape) — every Korean home has at least one jar quietly working in a corner. The longer the wait, the smoother the result.
stories.didYouKnow: A bottle of homemade maesilju aged 10 years can sell for more than commercial whisky.

stories.title: Korea's Whisky Moment
stories.body: The premium tier. Rice or grain spirit distilled to high proof and aged in clay onggi jars. Andong Soju, Munbaeju, Hwayo, the temple-aged Songhwa Baekiljoo — the headliners. After decades eclipsed by mass soju, they're now positioned as Korea's answer to single-malt whisky, and tasting menus are taking notice.
stories.didYouKnow: The clay onggi jar gives Korean spirits their unique aging character — porous walls let micro-air exchange, similar to oak in whisky.

stories.title: The Living Edge
stories.body: Some sools defy the standard categories. Dansul (sweet, near-zero-alcohol rice drink for kids and elders), Dongdongju (rice grains floating on top), regional one-offs only made in three villages, modern bombs like somaek (소맥). This is where Korean drinking culture stays alive and weird. Most disappear, a few become the next big thing.
stories.didYouKnow: The white floating grains in Dongdongju are called 동동 because they 'float-float' on top — pure onomatopoeia.
